KYC verification: how banks verify identity

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 23, 2026•8 min read

KYC verification is the step where a bank or fintech checks the identifying information a new customer gave, so it can form a reasonable belief about who the customer is. In the US, the rule for banks is the customer identification program requirement at 31 CFR 1020.220. It asks for risk-based procedures that "enable the bank to form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of each customer." The bank collects the information before it opens the account and verifies it within a reasonable time after.

This guide covers the methods the rule allows, failed checks, vendors, deepfakes and how an operations team runs the work. It explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What KYC verification has to prove

The standard is a reasonable belief about who the customer is. The 2005 interagency CIP guidance says a bank does not have to establish the accuracy of every piece of identifying information. It must verify enough of it to form that reasonable belief.

The procedures are risk-based. The rule tells a bank to base them on the types of accounts it offers, how accounts are opened, the identifying information available, and its own size, location and customer base.

Verification works from the minimum set the bank collects before opening: name, date of birth for an individual, address, and an identification number, which for a US person is a taxpayer identification number (TIN). Our guide to what KYC means in banking covers the wider program.

Documentary and non-documentary methods

The rule gives two main ways to verify, and the written procedures must say when the bank uses documents, non-documentary methods or both.

MethodWhat the rule listsFurther detail
Documents, individualUnexpired government-issued identification evidencing nationality or residence and bearing a photograph or similar safeguard, such as a driver's license or passportOther forms of ID may be used if they support a reasonable belief. Given counterfeits, the FFIEC manual says "a bank is encouraged to review more than a single document"
Documents, entityDocuments showing the entity exists, such as certified articles of incorporation, a government-issued business license, a partnership agreement or a trust instrumentThe procedures must name the documents the bank will accept
Non-documentaryContacting the customer; comparing what the customer gave with a consumer reporting agency, public database or other source; checking references with other financial institutions; obtaining a financial statementAn electronic credential, such as a digital certificate, can be one of the methods for an account opened online
Additional verificationFor a customer that is not an individual, information about individuals with authority or control over the account, including signatoriesUsed only when documents and non-documentary methods cannot verify the customer

The rule says a bank's non-documentary procedures must address five situations. The first is an individual who cannot present an unexpired photo ID. The others are documents the bank is not familiar with, an account opened without obtaining documents, a customer who does not appear in person, and other circumstances that raise the risk that documents alone will not verify identity. Every account opened online is one of these, so the procedures have to say how the bank verifies it.

Other KYC checks that run alongside verification

"KYC checks" often means the whole onboarding bundle. Only some of it is identity verification under the rule.

  • Beneficial owners. For a legal entity customer, 31 CFR 1010.230 requires verifying the identity of each beneficial owner with risk-based procedures that contain at least the CIP elements for individuals. For documentary checks, the rule lets the institution use photocopies or other reproductions. Our KYC guide covers the 2026 FinCEN order on when that work is repeated for an existing customer, and KYB verification covers owner mapping.
  • Government list comparison. The CIP rule requires a check against any list of known or suspected terrorists that Treasury designates for CIP purposes. The FFIEC manual notes: "As of the publication date of this Manual, no designated government lists for CIP purposes exist."
  • Sanctions screening. The manual says OFAC checks and section 314(a) requests "remain separate and distinct requirements". Our guide to reviewing a sanctions screening hit covers that work.

When identity cannot be verified

Every CIP must include procedures for when the bank cannot form a reasonable belief that it knows the customer's true identity. Under the rule, those procedures should describe:

  1. When the bank should not open an account.
  2. The terms under which a customer may use an account while the bank attempts to verify identity.
  3. When the bank should close an account after attempts to verify have failed.
  4. When the bank should file a suspicious activity report.

The rule's record requirements include "a description of the resolution of any substantive discrepancy discovered when verifying the identifying information obtained." In practice that means the procedure defines which mismatches are substantive, such as a date of birth that does not match the source, and which are not, such as a known abbreviation in a street name. It also names who clears each kind.

Using a KYC verification service

Document checks, database matching, selfie and liveness tools, or a full KYC verification service can all come from a vendor, and some firms buy KYC services for the whole step. The FFIEC manual says the CIP rule "does not alter a bank's authority to use a third party, such as an agent or service provider", but "the bank is ultimately responsible for compliance with the requirements of the CIP rule." The interagency guidance makes the same point for electronic credentials: "the bank is responsible for ensuring that the third party uses the same level of authentication as the bank itself would use."

Formal reliance on another financial institution works differently. A bank may rely on another institution, including an affiliate, to perform parts of its CIP for a customer that also has an account or similar formal relationship with that institution. The reliance must be reasonable, and the other institution must have its own AML program rule and a federal functional regulator. It must also sign a contract to certify each year that it has implemented its AML program and will perform the specified CIP requirements. The interagency guidance draws the line for agents such as a mortgage broker or car dealer: "In contrast to the reliance provision in the CIP rule, the bank is ultimately responsible for its agent's compliance". Our guide to what KYC software needs to do lists questions to ask a vendor.

TIN collection changed in 2025. In an order dated June 27, 2025, the OCC, FDIC and NCUA, with FinCEN's concurrence, let the banks they supervise obtain TIN information from a third-party source instead of from the customer. The Federal Reserve Board issued a matching order on July 31, 2025. Under the first order, "The use of this exemption by banks is optional", and a bank that uses it "must still obtain the full TIN from a third-party source prior to opening an account". Before this, the rule allowed third-party sourcing only for credit card accounts.

Deepfakes and forged identity documents

In alert FIN-2024-Alert004 (November 13, 2024), FinCEN said that from 2023 it observed more suspicious activity reports describing suspected deepfake media, often altered or generated identity documents used to get past identity verification. It said institutions "often detect GenAI and synthetic content in identity documents by conducting re-reviews of a customer's account opening documents."

In its section on detecting deepfake identity documents, the alert lists indicators that more scrutiny might be warranted, while noting they are not conclusive on their own:

  • Inconsistencies among multiple identity documents submitted by the customer.
  • A customer who cannot satisfactorily authenticate their identity, source of income or another part of their profile.
  • Inconsistencies between the identity document and other parts of the customer's profile.

FinCEN names multifactor authentication and live verification checks, where a customer confirms identity through audio or video, as practices that may reduce exposure. It notes that someone using a deepfake identity may claim repeated technical glitches or ask to change how they communicate during a check. A verification procedure can treat those behaviors as a reason to route the application to a reviewer. FinCEN asks for the key term "FIN-2024-DEEPFAKEFRAUD" in SAR field 2 and the narrative when a report relates to the alert.

How a bank or fintech team runs KYC verification

  1. Write the method per channel. For each customer type and way of opening an account, set which documents are accepted, which non-documentary sources are used, and when both apply. Cover the five situations the rule names for non-documentary methods.
  2. Define pass, fail and discrepancy. List the fields that must match, the tolerance for each, which mismatches are substantive, and who can clear them.
  3. Collect for the method. Show the CIP notice and capture what the chosen method needs: the identifying information, document images or the data a database check matches against.
  4. Run the checks. Send documents and data to the verification sources the procedure names. For a business, verify the entity and each beneficial owner.
  5. Review exceptions. Route failed checks, substantive discrepancies and deepfake indicators to a named reviewer, who works the case under the lack-of-verification procedure and records which outcome applied.
  6. Record the result. Keep the identifying information, a description of each document relied on (type, number, place of issuance and dates), the non-documentary methods and their results, and how each substantive discrepancy was resolved.
  7. Re-review when risk changes. Look again at the account opening file when later activity raises questions, as the FinCEN alert describes, and refresh information through a periodic KYC review.

In Verkflo's KYC onboarding review, part of its KYC automation, an AI agent checks applicant data from Sumsub against the team's written procedure and pauses for a reviewer where the procedure says.

Common questions

Does a bank have to verify identity before it opens the account?

The identifying information has to be obtained before the account opens. Verification can be completed within a reasonable time after opening, and the procedures set the terms for using the account while it is pending.

Does a bank have to keep a copy of the ID?

No. The FFIEC manual says a bank may keep copies but the CIP rule does not require it. The bank must keep a description of the document, and keep those records for five years after they are made.

Is KYC verification the same as identity verification?

Yes, in the CIP sense: KYC identity verification is the CIP step. KYC as a whole also covers beneficial owners, the customer risk profile, screening and ongoing monitoring.

Can a vendor do KYC verification for us?

Yes. A bank can use a service provider to verify customers, but it stays ultimately responsible for compliance with the CIP rule, so it needs to know the provider's methods meet its own procedures.

Sources

  • 31 CFR 1020.220, customer identification program requirements for banks
  • 31 CFR 1010.230, beneficial ownership requirements for legal entity customers
  • FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual, Customer Identification Program
  • Interagency Interpretive Guidance on Customer Identification Program Requirements under Section 326 of the USA PATRIOT Act (April 28, 2005)
  • OCC, FDIC and NCUA order on TIN collection from a third-party source (June 27, 2025) and the Federal Reserve Board order (July 31, 2025)
  • FinCEN Alert on Fraud Schemes Involving Deepfake Media Targeting Financial Institutions, FIN-2024-Alert004 (November 13, 2024)
